Shape.Name: procedure
Shape.Text:
Very often it's not the system but the way it's being used that causes low SNR images. If the reported problems are only occurring on certain studies, it is quite possible that the customer has altered the scan protocol in a way that influences SNR.
Protocol changes which will reduce SNR: A decrease in slice thickness, decrease in field of view, or increase in Imaging Matrix size all decrease the voxel size in the image and thereby reduce SNR Reducing the number of NEX will reduce SNR due to the loss of signal averaging Reduction in inter scan space (skip) within a single acquisition will reduce signal through inter-slice crosstalk Reducing a scan's TR will increase spin saturation and result in lower signal Increasing a scan's TE will reduce image to SNR due to T2 and T2* dephasing Reducing the scan's TE below the minimum full echo level will generate a lower SNR since only a fraction of the echo is being sampled and this results in less signal data. Increasing the Image Variable Bandwith will result in lower SNR due to the additional noise frequencies in the wider bandwidth

Shape.Name: Create request
Shape.Text:
Try to find some old images from when the Image Quality was acceptable to compare the current images to. If this is not possible, you will have to use the “Picture This” or GE default “canned” protocols to make comparisons.
Image compare : Display the “reference” and “suspected” images on the same monitor, preferably side by side using the image display “compare” mode. Start out using identical window and level settings. Look for a big difference in the image intensity and / or noise. During the compare process, make sure that the imaging parameters are IDENTICAL!! Even small, seemingly insignificant, changes in the scan protocol can cause drastically different image quality.

Shape.Name: procedure
Shape.Text: Parameters Affecting SNR (excerpted from SUN Vol. V No. 1 Feb. 1989) What is SNR? SNR is the ratio of the MR signal to the noise. To increase the ratio you need to increase signal or decrease noise. For Example, if the signal amplitude is 100 and the noise level is 10 the SNR would be 100/10 or 10. In another example, if the signal amplitude is 50 and the noise level is constant at 10 the SNR would be 50/10 or 5. The image with an SNR of 10 would no doubt be more pleasing to the eye than the 5 SNR image (assuming other parameters are constant). Viewing an image with a low SNR is somewhat like looking through a dirty window versus a clean window. If the signal is not great enough (the SNR is too low), the boundaries between tissues may be obscured and thus degrade the image's diagnostic utility. Signal to noise ratio dependencies on volume and sample time can be expressed with an equation that states: "SNR IS PROPORTIONAL TO THE VOXEL VOLUME TIMES THE SQUARE ROOT OF THE TOTAL SAMPLING TIME". These two SNR terms can be thought of as space (or resolution) and time. What is sampling time? The total sampling time is determined by a number of factors which also affect the total scan time: TOTAL SAMPLING TIME = NEX x Ny x (Nx / BW) where: NEX = the number of excitations Nx = the number of samples in the frequency direction Ny = the number of views in the phase direction BW = bandwidth or sampling frequency fro frequency encoding. What is the voxel volume? The height and width of the voxel volume is determined by the pixel size and the depth is measured by the slice thickness. VOXEL VOLUME = SLT x (FOV x / Nx) x (FOV y / Ny) where: SLT = slice thickness Nx = the number of samples in the frequency direction Ny = the number of views in the phase direction FOV x = field of view in the frequency direction FOV y = field of view in the phase direction

Shape.Text:
In order for you to help your customer understand what effect on SNR various changes in scan protocol have you will need to be able to:
compare SNR between similar sequence types act as a guide to help choose image parameters help optimize tradeoffs between spatial resolution and SNR.
It is suggested that you obtain a copy of "SUN" (Signa Users' Newsletter) Volume V No. 1 Feb. 1989. This edition was devoted entirely to SNR in MR imaging and is a useful tutorial for anyone requiring the tools for assessing the changes that occur when certain parameters are altered.
For a brief excerpt from the above SUN article, read the THEORY section.

Shape.Name: procedure
Shape.Text:
Considering how common spike noise is, and how easy it is to inadvertently create it, even in the controlled environment of an RF screen room; GE design engineers searched for a means to make the Signa MRI system less sensitive and reduce the vulnerability to their inevitable occurrence. A few different schemes were considered, but eventually it was decided that their approach would be a hardware solution that would detect and "blank out" spikes before they even reached the MR receiver. The name of this device was originally the Transient Noise Suppressor (TNS) but that was later changed to Transient Noise Filter (TNF). It is actually the exact same device.
New Excite 2A (11.0 M3a) and later systems have a completely redesigned TNF, called the Universal TNS (UTNS3). The concept is very promising in that the UTNS will have a separate antenna in the scan room and it's own "receiver" just for detecting broadband events. For the remainder of this discussion we will be referring to the old "tried and true" TNF that we have come to know and love, which is currently installed in the vast majority of the installed base.
Physically, the TNFs are located in the Systems cabinet. Functionally, they are located between the preamplifiers and receivers in each receive channel. There will normally be one TNF Assembly with multiple TNF channels, one for each receive channel. Multi-coil systems will have a 3-channel TNF expansion module, which piggybacks to the original 2-channel TNF assembly.
First, the input signal is split. Part of it goes through a notch filter, which is centered on the nominal magnet frequency. This filter will reject signals a set bandwidth above and below the nominal magnet frequency, but pass any other received signals. This is what prevents the TNF from detecting and blanking the desired NMR signal.
An Enable / Disable switch is provided in the TNF Assembly to control the detection and blanking of all channels. When enabled, the filtered signal goes to the Spike Detection circuit of the TNF channel. Any signal that gets past the Notch Filter, since we have established that it is not an NMR signal, must be broadband noise and will therefore be detected. Spikes thusly detected will trigger actuation of the Transient Blanker Switch. When the blanker switch is actuated it interrupts the normal signal path and places a nominal impedance on the receive line. This is so the receive signal does not drop to zero when blanked, which would itself cause problems in the reconstructed images, but will instead go to some nominal noise value for the duration.
The Spike Detector also sends a signal to the TNF event counter. There is only one counter for all TNF channels in the assembly. The counter will only increment once for any simultaneously detected spike on the multiple TNF channels. However, keep in mind that each TNF channel is capable of detecting and blanking independently. The event counter will also only increment if the "Data in Window" and "Receiver Unblank" signals are both true (high). Note that these control signals have the effect of only gating the counter. A detected spike event will still actuate the Transient Blanker Switch regardless of the state of the "Data in Window" and "Receiver Unblank" signals.

Shape.Name: procedure
Shape.Text:
The split input signal path from the preamplifiers that does not go thru the notch filter is the normal receive signal path. This signal is amplified in a Gain Stage to compensate for the insertion losses of the rest of the circuitry. The net overall gain of the circuit should still be 1:1.
By the time the Spike Detector is able to sense a noise impulse and the Transient Blanker Switch is actuated, the spike would likely already be halfway to the receiver. To combat this, a delay function is added to the normal signal path. This aligns the blanking relative to the spike noise for complete suppression.
A 15-volt preamplifier bias is output on the RF input cable of each channel, at all times. There is also a DC block on the RF Output circuit of each channel to prevent loading down the preamplifier bias supply circuit of the transceiver.

Shape.Name: procedure
Shape.Text:
TNF Troubleshooting
There are many things that can go wrong with the TNF that will cause problems with the imaging system. Since there are many active components in the design, it is entirely possible for the TNS to negatively effect the receive signal even when there is no spike noise present, or the switch is placed in the “Disable” position. Either low gain or a noisy TNF channel can negatively impact image quality through reduced SNR. A channel with excessive gain has been seen to be the cause “Over-ranged Receiver” images as the example at left.
The first logical step in troubleshooting a suspected bad TNS is to bypass the questionable channel (or channels) by connecting the TNS Input cable to the TNS Output cable using a BNC bullet connector.
If the symptoms change, you will know that you are on the right track. However, this does not necessarily prove that the TNF is faulty. You need to be aware that it is possible for the TNF to sense an “out of band” signal, which it would interpret to be broadband noise, but which is actually some other discrete (correlated) noise that happens in that frequency range. You should use the SPT correlated noise test (with the TNS bypassed) to be sure.
You should also be aware that excessive spike noise in the scan room can, and will, cause ghosting in images due to an excess of the desired NMR signal being blanked. This may be mistaken as a faulty TNS when, in reality, the TNS is functioning exactly as designed to. The simple test to rule this out is to place the TNS in the “Disable” position and scan. If the problem is due to excessive blanking the images will go from being ghosted to having corduroy or other image noise problems, at which point you could begin chasing white pixels.
Of course, a TNF could also malfunction such that it no longer blanks when it should, when spike noise does occur. This would be evident as corduroy artifact in images even when the TNF is in circuit and enabled. The TNF assembly has a built-in spike generator, and a Functional test procedure has been developed and documented on the MR Service Methods CD ROM to functionally test each TNF channel.

Shape.Name: Create request
Shape.Text:
The SNR subtest can fail for an improper TG. To determine if this is the case you will need to determine the proper TG range for your system. To do this you will need to view the SPT spec file for SNR. The file is located in the “/usr/g/service/cclass/spt” directory and is named “snr.spt”.
Below is an example of this file:
# Rev 1.3 created on 02/20/98 # 1.5T Echo Speed, High Speed & Horizon SNR Limits # marginal severe # low high lowlow highhigh h_head_signal 0 10000.0 0 10000.0 h_head_noise n/a 10000.0 n/a 10000.0 h_head_snr 42.7 n/a 40.4 n/a h_head_tg 47 85 32 100 h_body_signal 0 10000.0 0 10000.0 h_body_noise n/a 10000.0 n/a 10000.0 h_body_snr 24.37 n/a 23.09 n/a h_body_tg 110 140 95 155
Note the two lines “h_head_tg” and “h_body_tg”. These are the specs for TG for head and body respectively. Compare your test results to these ranges to determine if the system is operating in the TG nominal range.

A non-linearity can cause the RF output to be out of range when scanning at nominal TGs even though it is correct at full Power. It can also cause distortion in the RF waveform, which would result in Low SNR in certain scan types. Unfortunately, the only way to do this is via the RFT procedure, which can be found in the MR Service Methods.
Set up for the “Sense Loop” mode of whichever coil is failing SPT TG range. Make sure the RF linearity subtest is selected in the User cv’s.

Shape.Name: Create request.6
Shape.Text:
Determining whether “High Noise” or “Low Signal” was the cause for the low SNR condition requires comparing to an old, passing run of SPT SNR subtest. In order to make the comparison, both the current and old runs must have been scanned with the same “System Gain” values.
Compare System Gain in the two reports. If they are not the same, change the System gain for the coil of interest to the value reported in the old file and repeat the SPT SNR subtest so we can get equivalent data.
Once we have a current subtest run at the same System Gain as the previously passing SPT run, we can make a direct “apples to apples” comparison. Is the reduction in SNR due to an increase in the noise level or a decrease in signal?
If you can not find an old passing SPT run, for example if this is a new install, we will have to rule out both possibilities, which will take longer.

Perform the Proprietary “Noise Only Test” or “System Noise Floor Test” to determine background noise level. Use these tests as a gauge while troubleshooting to find the noise source.
If only one coil is failing SNR, this could be caused by a noisy preamp or other hardware in the failing receive-chain. It is also possible that if only the head coil fails that this is because of its higher sensitivity due to the higher coil q.
Look for high background noise levels caused by electrical equipment inside the RF screen room. Try to turn everything off possible and repeat the Noise test.
You can also use the Noise test to try and “sniff out” the noise test. Put the head coil on a longer than normal receive cable and move the coil to various locations in the scan room repeating the test, comparing the results for the location with the highest amplitude.
If both coils fail it is remotely possible a bad receiver could be at fault.

Shape.Text:
Certain scan sequences are more SNR susceptible to eddy currents. Is the customer’s complaint with scans done with a Gradient Echo, EPI (including DWEPI or SSFSE) or other Fast Spin Echo sequence? If so, we will want to run the eddy current compensation procedure to make an analysis of the state of compensation.
Standard Spin Echo (MEMP) scans are not very sensitive to eddy current compensation. If the customer is complaining about MEMP sequences and you have not found the problem by this point in the flowchart you should ask for additional technical support now.
